## 12. Versioning & Scope

### Versioning

The `version` field in every event enables future protocol evolution. Zentty will:

- Accept `version: 1` indefinitely.
- Reject events with unknown versions (non-zero exit code, error on stderr).
- Document breaking changes under a new version number.

### What's Not in the Protocol

- **OSC 9;4 progress sequences** — Terminal escape sequences for progress bars. Zentty reads these from the terminal emulator layer, not from the agent protocol. Agents that emit OSC 9;4 get running-state detection for free, and panes without an agent show them as a program status (see [Program Status](program-status.md)), but they're not part of this protocol.
- **Terminal title heuristics** — Zentty parses terminal titles to detect agent state when no hook is available. This is a fallback mechanism, not a protocol feature.
- **Desktop notification signals** — Zentty recognizes certain desktop notification patterns as agent state signals. This is also a fallback, not part of the protocol.

# Agent Teams and tmux-based agent tools

Some agent tools run their teammates or subagents in tmux panes. Zentty ships a small `tmux` command that answers those tools from inside a Zentty pane, so each teammate shows up as a Zentty pane rather than in a tmux session you can't see. The first teammate opens a column to the right of the pane that started the team; later teammates stack in that column. Closing the lead pane closes its teammates.

This is experimental. Nothing gets installed into your agent configs or your real tmux. The tmux command only exists for the processes Zentty starts in team mode.

## Turning it on

You can turn it on in two ways.

**For one launch.** Start the tool from a Zentty pane:

```bash
zentty launch --teams claude          # Claude Code with agent teams on
zentty launch claude --teams          # same thing
zentty launch --tmux-shim -- omx team 3:executor "fix the failing tests"
zentty launch --tmux-shim             # a login shell in team mode; run any tmux-based tool from it
```

`--teams <agent>` launches an integrated agent the normal way (status hooks included) with the tmux command on `PATH`. For Claude Code it also sets `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`. `--teams` must come before the agent's own arguments.

`--tmux-shim [--] [command …]` runs any command that way. Without a command you get your login shell, and everything you start from it sees the same tmux.

**For every new pane.** Turn on **Settings → Agents → Agent teams**, or set it in `~/.config/zentty/config.toml`:

```toml
[agent_teams]
enabled = true
```

New panes then start in team mode with Claude Code's team switch on. Panes that were already open keep their old environment. If Zentty itself was started from inside a real tmux session, it leaves that session's `TMUX` alone.

Inside Zentty the team switch wins over Claude Code's own settings. Claude normally lets an `env` entry in `~/.claude/settings.json` override the environment, so a `"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "0"` there would turn teams back off. In team-mode panes Zentty also puts `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in the settings it passes to Claude, which take precedence. With the setting off, Zentty leaves the variable alone.

## Tools

| Tool | How to start it | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code agent teams | `zentty launch --teams claude`, or the Settings toggle | Uses Claude's tmux teammate mode. If you set `teammateMode` to `in-process` in Claude's settings, teammates stay in Claude's own UI. |
| oh-my-claudecode (`omc team …`) | `zentty launch --tmux-shim -- omc team 2:claude "…"` | Workers open as panes in the current worklane. |
| oh-my-codex (`omx team …`) | `zentty launch --tmux-shim -- omx team 3:executor "…"` | Its HUD pane lands in the teammate column too. |
| oh-my-openagent / oh-my-opencode | `zentty launch --tmux-shim -- opencode` | Set `"tmux": { "enabled": true }` in its config. Use `isolation: "inline"` or `"window"`; detached sessions are not shown. For team mode also set `team_mode.tmux_visualization`. |
| Codex CLI | not needed | Codex has no tmux teammate mode. |

## What the tmux command understands

Zentty maps tmux's model onto its own: the Zentty window is the tmux session, each worklane is a tmux window, each pane a tmux pane. A `new-window` pane opens in the teammate column too, but tools see it, and the panes later split from it, as a window of its own, so one tool's window commands don't reach another tool's panes. Pane, window and session ids are numeric (`%3`, `@1`, `$0`) like tmux's. `tmux -V` reports `tmux 3.4`.

| Area | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| Creating panes | `split-window`, `new-window` (title from `-n`), `new-session -P`, with `-c`, `-e NAME=VALUE`, `-d`, `-P -F`, a command as one string or as argv |
| Driving panes | `send-keys` (key names, `-l`, `--`), `respawn-pane` (deferred or live with `-k`; the pane keeps its id), `select-pane -T`, `kill-pane`, `capture-pane -p` |
| Reading state | `display-message -p`, `list-panes [-a\|-s]`, `list-windows`, `list-sessions`, `has-session`, `show-options` |
| Options | `set-option` / `set-window-option` with `-p`, `-w`, `-g`, `-s`, `-a`, `-u`, `-o`, `-F`; user options (`@name`) read back by `show-options` and `#{@name}` |
| Command lines | `cmd ; cmd` sequences, `if-shell [-F]`, `run-shell [-b] [-C]`, `wait-for` |
| Targets | `%N`, `@N`, `$N`, `session:window.pane`, `=name`, indexes and names |
| Formats | `#{var}`, `#{?cond,a,b}`, `#{==:a,b}`, `#{!=:…}`, `#{<:…}` and friends, `#{&&:…}`, `#{\|\|:…}`, `#{m:…}`, `#{=N:…}`, `#{b:…}`, `#{d:…}`, `#{q:…}`, `#S` / `#I` / `#P` / `#D` / `#T` |
| Format variables | `pane_id`, `pane_index`, `pane_title`, `pane_active`, `pane_pid`, `pane_dead`, `pane_current_path`, `pane_current_command`, `pane_start_command`, `pane_width`, `pane_height`, `window_id`, `window_index`, `window_name`, `window_width`, `window_height`, `session_id`, `session_name`, `session_created`, `socket_path`, `pid`, `version` and more |

Missing targets fail like tmux: `can't find pane: %9` on stderr and exit status 1. A command without `-t` from a pane that no longer exists fails the same way instead of acting on another pane.

`-P` without `-F` prints a target that keeps naming the new pane (`zentty:@4.%7` for `split-window`, `zentty:@9` for `new-window`), where tmux would print window and pane positions that shift when you add or close panes.

Zentty keeps control of focus and layout. `select-layout` and `resize-pane` only rebalance the teammate column. `select-window`, `rename-window`, `set-hook`, `switch-client`, `kill-session` and `kill-server` succeed and change nothing, so a tool's cleanup can't close your own panes. For the same reason `kill-pane` and `respawn-pane -k` only act on the calling pane and on panes the tmux command created; on any other pane they succeed and change nothing. `kill-window` only closes panes the tmux command created in that window, never the pane that started the team, and `kill-pane -a` is ignored. Unknown commands also succeed and do nothing.

Not supported: attaching to detached sessions, copy mode, popups (`display-popup` fails), key bindings, and exact tmux layouts and sizes. Pane sizes are reported in cells but are approximate.

## Troubleshooting

Set `ZENTTY_TMUX_COMPAT_TRACE_PATH` to a file before launching and every tmux call is logged there as JSON lines. Panes opened with the Settings toggle on log to `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/tmux-compat-trace.jsonl` (`Zentty Dev` for the dev build) by default.

`pane_pid` comes from the pane's shell. A pane whose command does not run through a supported login shell (zsh, bash or fish) may report it empty.

# Zentty CLI

Zentty includes an embedded `zentty` CLI for scripting windows, worklanes, and panes.

Most commands must run inside a Zentty pane because they use pane environment variables such as `ZENTTY_INSTANCE_SOCKET`, `ZENTTY_WINDOW_ID`, `ZENTTY_WORKLANE_ID`, `ZENTTY_PANE_ID`, and `ZENTTY_PANE_TOKEN`. Commands that target another pane can use selector flags when a control token is available.

## Open a Folder From Outside Zentty

To open a new window at a directory from a script, a URL handler, or another app, hand the folder to Zentty through LaunchServices:

```bash
open -a Zentty ~/Development/my-project
```

This reaches the running instance, or launches Zentty first if it is not running. Finder's "Open With" and dropping a folder on the Dock icon do the same. A file opens its parent folder.

## Common Selectors

Pane and layout commands accept these selector flags unless noted otherwise:

- `--window-id <window-id>`: target a specific window.
- `--worklane-id <worklane-id>`: target a specific worklane.
- `--pane-id <pane-id>`: target a specific pane by ID.
- `--pane-index <pane-index>`: target a specific 1-based pane index within the selected worklane.
- `--pane-token <pane-token>`: authorize out-of-pane control. The token only authenticates; it does not pick the pane. Outside the target pane, also pass `--pane-id` (or `--worklane-id` / `--window-id`) to say which pane you mean.

Discovery commands accept:

- `--window-id <window-id>`: filter by window.
- `--worklane-id <worklane-id>`: filter by worklane.
- `--include-control-token`: include pane control tokens in JSON output.
- `--json`: output JSON.

## Version

Show the running Zentty version and bundled git commit.

```bash
zentty version
```

## Discovery

List windows, worklanes, and panes.

```bash
zentty list [--window-id <window-id>] [--worklane-id <worklane-id>] [--include-control-token] [--json]
zentty list windows [--json]
zentty list worklanes [--window-id <window-id>] [--worklane-id <worklane-id>] [--include-control-token] [--json]
zentty list panes [--window-id <window-id>] [--worklane-id <worklane-id>] [--include-control-token] [--json]
```

Aliases:

```bash
zentty window list [--json]
zentty worklane list [--window-id <window-id>] [--worklane-id <worklane-id>] [--include-control-token] [--json]
zentty pane list [--window-id <window-id>] [--worklane-id <worklane-id>] [--include-control-token] [--json]
```

`zentty pane list` defaults to the calling pane's current worklane when no window or worklane filter is provided. Use `zentty list panes` for broader discovery.

Examples:

```bash
zentty list
zentty list panes --json
zentty list panes --worklane-id wl_123 --include-control-token --json
```

Resolve a single pane target and print its IDs.

### Send Text

Type text into a pane, then press Enter.

```bash
zentty pane send [<pane-index|pane-id>] [--no-enter] [--paste] [--force] [selectors] -- <text...>
```

The text after `--` is typed as if from the keyboard. Without `--`, the text is read from stdin when stdin is a pipe or a file, and one trailing newline is dropped. Empty text is an error, so an empty variable never turns into a bare Enter; to press Enter alone, use `pane send-key <pane> Enter`. Enter follows after a short pause, so programs that read input in chunks see a submit instead of a pasted newline.

Text with more than one line is always delivered as a paste, so a shell does not run each line as it arrives.

- `--no-enter`: type the text without pressing Enter.
- `--paste`: deliver the text as a paste. The program receives a bracketed paste when it asked for one.
- `--force`: send even when the agent in the target pane is mid-turn or showing a prompt.

The destination must be named, with a positional pane index or ID, or with `--pane-id`, `--pane-index`, or `--worklane-id`. To send to your own pane, pass its ID.

If an agent in the target pane is mid-turn, or is showing an approval, decision, or sign-in prompt, the command fails and sends nothing unless you pass `--force`. Typed characters can act as menu hotkeys in those prompts, and Enter picks the highlighted option. An agent asking a question or waiting for plain input, an idle agent, and a stopped agent are fine to send to. A pane whose terminal has not started yet, for example right after a restore, fails with `pane_unavailable` instead of losing the text.

Examples:

```bash
zentty pane send 2 -- npm test
zentty pane send 2 --no-enter -- 'git commit -m "'
git diff | zentty pane send 3 --paste
zentty pane send --pane-id pn_123 --pane-token "$TOKEN" -- yes
```

`pane send-key` follows the same agent rule as `pane send`, and `--force` overrides it. `C-c` and `Escape` on their own always go through, so interrupting an agent never needs `--force`.

```bash

zentty pane send-key 2 Up Enter
zentty pane send-key --pane-id pn_123 --pane-token "$TOKEN" Escape
```

## Events

Stream workspace events until interrupted.

```bash
zentty events [--json] [--type <type>]... [selectors]
```

- `--json`: print one JSON object per line (NDJSON). Without it, each event is one readable line.
- `--type <type>`: only events of this type (`agent.phase`) or family (`pane`, also written `pane.*`). Repeat it to select several. A name that matches no event type fails.

Every JSON event has a versioned envelope, `{"v":1,"type":"...","ts":"..."}`, with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps. The other fields depend on the type, and absent fields are left out:

| Type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `stream.ready` | First line. Every change after it is reported. |
| `stream.dropped` | `count`. Events were dropped because the reader fell behind. |
| `worklane.created`, `worklane.closed` | `window`, `worklane` |
| `worklane.activated` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane` |
| `pane.created`, `pane.closed`, `pane.focused` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane` |
| `pane.moved` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane`, `from_worklane` |
| `agent.phase` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane`, `agent`, `phase`, `previous_phase`, `interaction` |
| `attention.raised` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane`, `agent`, `attention`, `interaction` |
| `attention.cleared` | `window`, `worklane`, `pane`, `agent`, `previous_attention` |

`pane.focused` reports a worklane's focused pane changing, in background worklanes too. `worklane.activated` reports a window switching to another worklane, with that worklane's focused pane. Together they tell which pane each window shows.

`phase` is `starting`, `running`, `needs-input`, `unresolved-stop`, `idle`, or `exited` when the agent leaves the pane. `interaction` is `approval`, `question`, `decision`, `auth`, or `generic-input` while an agent needs input. `attention` is `needs-input`, `unresolved-stop`, `ready`, or `check-back`.

The stream covers every window of the Zentty instance the command talks to, and only that instance. It needs a pane token, like the pane commands: inside a pane the environment provides one, and from outside pass `--pane-id` and `--pane-token`. A reader that stops reading loses events rather than slowing Zentty down, and finds a `stream.dropped` line with the count when it catches up.

Examples:

```bash
zentty events --json --type agent.phase --type attention
zentty events --json | jq -c 'select(.type == "attention.raised")'
```

## Agent History

Search earlier Claude Code, Codex, Grok and opencode sessions that Agent History has indexed. Run these from a Zentty pane, with Agent History turned on in Settings › Agent History. [Agent History settings](configuration.md#agent-history-settings) explains what the index holds and what it redacts.

```bash
zentty history search <query...> [--all] [--agent <name>] [--limit <n>] [--json]
zentty history show <session-id> [--all] [--agent <name>] [--turns <n>] [--json]
```

- `search` matches session titles, branches, repository and folder names, the files, commands, commits and pull requests a session touched, and the conversation itself. The query takes the palette's operators: `agent:`, `repo:`, `branch:`, `before:YYYY-MM-DD` and `after:YYYY-MM-DD`. Dates are local; `before:` leaves that day out and `after:` includes it. Text in double quotes is matched as one phrase, so quote it for the shell too: `'"connection reset"'`. A query can be up to 200 characters. Put terms that start with `-` after `--`. `--limit` defaults to 10 and goes up to 50.
- `show` prints the most recent turns of one session, oldest first. `--turns` defaults to 20 and goes up to 200. A turn over 4 KB is cut and marked `[truncated]`. If the answer would still be too large, the oldest turns are dropped and the output says how many it shows.
- `--agent <name>`: only sessions from `claude`, `codex`, `grok` or `opencode`. For `show`, use it when two agents have a session with the same ID; without it you get the one updated most recently.
- `--all`: look in every project. This only works when **Allow agents to search all projects** is on in Settings › Agent History. It's off by default.
- `--json`: print JSON instead of text.

Without `--all`, both commands only see sessions from the calling pane's project. In a git repository that's the repository and all its worktrees. Outside one, it's the pane's folder and the folders below it; in your home folder, only sessions started in the home folder itself count. The commands take no pane selectors, so the project always comes from the pane they run in. A pane on another machine has no local project, so only `--all` works there. Sessions you removed from Agent History and sessions in excluded folders never appear.

The text output lists each session with its agent, branch, folder, last update and `live` if it's running in a Zentty pane right now. Under that comes what matched (`You: …`, `Branch: …`, `Ran: …`) and a resume command (or the session ID when there is none). Titles, snippets and turns are quoted from past sessions. Control characters in them are printed escaped, and the output ends with a reminder to treat that text as data, not instructions.

JSON output uses ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and leaves out absent values:

- `search`: `scope` (`project` or `all`), `project` (the project's root folder), `indexedSessions`, `complete`, `contentIsUntrusted` (always `true`) and `results`. `complete` is `false` while the index is still being built, so older sessions may be missing. Each result has `agent`, `sessionId`, `title`, `cwd`, `branch`, `updatedAt`, `live`, `match` and `resumeCommand`. `match` is `{role, at, snippet}` when the conversation matched, otherwise `{field, value}` with `field` set to `title`, `branch`, `repo`, `folder`, `path`, `command`, `commit` or `pr`.
- `show`: `scope`, `project`, `agent`, `sessionId`, `title`, `cwd`, `branch`, `model`, `effort`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `live`, `totalTurns`, `omittedTurns`, `turns`, `resumeCommand` and `contentIsUntrusted`. Each turn has `role` (`user` or `agent`), `at`, `text` and `truncated`.

`resumeCommand` reopens the session in its agent. Run it from the session's folder (`cwd`). It's left out when Zentty can't build a safe resume command for the session.

Bad arguments, such as `--limit 99` or an unknown agent, fail with a usage error before the CLI contacts Zentty. Other failures print one line to stderr starting with `zentty history` and exit with a non-zero status:

| Situation | Message |
| --- | --- |
| Not run from a Zentty pane | `zentty history must run inside a Zentty pane.` |
| Agent History is off | `Agent History is turned off. …` |
| `--all` while the setting is off | `Searching all projects is turned off. …` |
| A remote pane, or a pane with no known folder | `… so its project is unknown.` |
| The session is unknown or outside the project | `No session <id> in this project's Agent History.` |
| The index is still starting, damaged, or from a newer Zentty | A line that says which, usually pointing to Settings › Agent History |
| `config.toml` was unreadable when Zentty started | `Agent History is paused because Zentty's config.toml can't be read, …` |
| No answer within about 5 seconds | `Agent History didn't answer in time. Try a narrower query.` |
| The running Zentty predates Agent History | `This Zentty version doesn't support Agent History. …` |

Examples:

```bash
zentty history search "virtual display timeout"
zentty history search agent:codex branch:feat/agent-history migration --json
zentty history show 3f2a9c1e-6d1b-4c7e-9a2f-0b1c2d3e4f50 --turns 40
```

# Configuration and Syncing

Zentty keeps everything you set up in `~/.config/zentty/`. That folder is safe to sync between Macs with Syncthing, a dotfiles repo, or similar, with one exception: the `run/` directory.

## What lives where

| Path | What it holds | Sync it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `~/.config/zentty/config.toml` | All app settings: sidebar, pane layout, appearance and theme, keyboard shortcuts, notifications, open-with apps, server detection, agent integration choices | Yes |
| `~/.config/zentty/bookmarks.json` | Saved worklane bookmarks | Yes, see [Bookmarks](#bookmarks) |
| `~/.config/zentty/sounds/` | Copies of custom notification sounds | Yes |
| `~/.config/zentty/agents/` | Your own agent definitions ([Agent Hooks](agent-hooks.md)) | Yes |
| `~/.config/zentty/run/` | The running app's socket, locks and agent wrapper scripts | **No** |
| `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/` | Session restore snapshot, saved pane output, agent session state | No |
| `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/AgentHistory/` | Agent History search index and its on/off state. Holds copies of your agent conversations, readable only by you and excluded from Time Machine | **No** |
| `~/Library/Preferences/be.zenjoy.zentty.plist` | Window positions, update checks | No |

The Zentty Dev build uses `~/.config/zentty-dev/` and `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty Dev/` instead.

## Syncing with Syncthing

Share `~/.config/zentty` and add this to its `.stignore`:

```
run
```

Zentty 0.3.7 and earlier kept session state in the same folder. Newer versions copy it out once and leave the old files in place, so add these too:

```
restore-snapshot.json
restore-lifecycle.json
tmux-compat-store.json
tmux-compat-trace.jsonl
```

Once every Mac runs a newer version, you can delete those four files from `~/.config/zentty`.

Don't sync the open windows and worklanes themselves. They belong to the Mac they run on, and each Mac restores its own session.

## How changes arrive

- **config.toml** reloads as soon as it changes on disk, so a setting changed on one Mac shows up on the other without a restart. This also works when `config.toml` is a symlink into another folder; Zentty writes through the link instead of replacing it.
- **bookmarks.json** reloads live too.
- **agents/** is read at launch. Restart Zentty after changing it.

If `config.toml` contains a line Zentty can't read, Zentty logs it and won't save over the file until you fix it. In the meantime it runs on its last good settings, or on defaults if the file was already broken at launch. Zentty also keeps sections and keys it doesn't recognize when it saves, so a Mac on an older version doesn't strip settings a newer version added. This works from the version after 0.3.7 onward; 0.3.7 and earlier treat an unknown section as a broken file and reset it to defaults on their next save, so keep shared Macs on the same version. Keys inside individual open-with apps, browsers and shortcut bindings aren't covered.

## Session restore

Zentty reopens your windows, worklanes and panes when it starts again, after a normal quit, an update relaunch, or a crash. Turn it off with **Restore worklanes on next launch** in Settings → General, or in `config.toml`:

```toml
[restore]
restore_workspace_on_launch = true
scrollback = true
```

`scrollback` (on by default, **Restore pane output** in Settings) brings back what each pane showed. When a pane comes back, its previous output is printed above the new prompt, followed by a dim `── restored from previous session ──` line. In an agent pane the agent resumes after that, the same way it does without saved output.

- Zentty saves the output when you quit. Every few minutes it also saves panes that are running a command or an agent, or that changed since the last save, so most of it survives a crash too.
- Each pane keeps its last 4,000 lines, up to about 1 MB, and older lines are dropped first. A save is capped at 32 MB in total, so with many panes each one keeps less.
- Only plain text is kept. Colors and other terminal control sequences are removed before saving, so printing the output again can't run anything.
- If a full-screen program such as vim or an agent's full-screen interface was open when the output was saved, the pane comes back with that program's last screen instead of the shell output behind it.
- The output is printed by Zentty's shell integration for zsh, bash, fish and nushell. Other shells, and shells started with `ZENTTY_SHELL_INTEGRATION=0`, come back without it.
- Saved output lives in `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/session-scrollback/`, one file per pane, readable only by you and excluded from Time Machine backups. Pane output can contain secrets. Zentty deletes a file once its pane is gone, and deletes all of them when you turn `scrollback` or session restore off.

If Zentty crashes twice in a row while reopening your workspace, it stops trying. A second Zentty that opens while the first is still reopening the workspace doesn't count as a crash. The next launch after two crashes opens a new window and renames the saved workspace to `restore-snapshot.set-aside-1.json` in `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/`, with a higher number if that name is taken. Zentty doesn't read that file again, and its saved output stays in `session-scrollback/`. You can delete both yourself, and turning `scrollback` or session restore off deletes the output.

If the rename fails, the saved workspace stays where it is and Zentty tells you so. Nothing writes over it or deletes it: each save tries the rename again first, and is skipped while that keeps failing, so the new windows aren't saved until it works. The next launch tries again too.

## Agent History settings

Agent History indexes your past Claude Code, Codex, Grok and opencode conversations so you can search and resume them from **Agent History…** (⌘⇧H) or with `zentty history` (see [CLI](cli.md)). It's off until you turn it on in Settings → Agent History, and it doesn't read any conversations before then.

Its settings live in two places.

Whether Agent History is on, and which agents it reads, belong to one Mac. They're kept in `state.json` inside `~/Library/Application Support/Zentty/AgentHistory/` and don't sync. Each Mac builds its own index and asks before reading anything.

Excluded folders and agent access are preferences, so they live in `config.toml` and sync with the rest of it:

```toml
[agent_history]
excluded_folders = ["~/Development/client-secrets", "~/notes"]
allow_agents_all_projects = false
```

- `excluded_folders`: Agent History never indexes a session whose working directory is inside one of these folders. Adding a folder removes its sessions from the index, and removing it lets them be read again. The check uses the folder the agent ran in, not the files it read, so a session started somewhere else that opened a file in an excluded folder is still indexed. Zentty writes paths under your home folder as `~/…`, so the list works on Macs with different user names.
- `allow_agents_all_projects` (**Allow agents to search all projects**, off by default): `zentty history` only sees sessions from the calling pane's project. Turn this on to let `--all` reach every project.

Keep `excluded_folders` on one line. Zentty reads `config.toml` a line at a time, so an array split over several lines makes the file unreadable, and Zentty won't save to it until you fix it (see [How changes arrive](#how-changes-arrive)).

If `config.toml` is unreadable when Zentty starts, Agent History can't tell which folders you excluded, so it pauses. It reads nothing new, and the palette and `zentty history` can't search until the file loads again. Indexing resumes as soon as you fix it. If the file breaks while Zentty is running, Agent History keeps the excluded folders it already had.

What the index holds:

- Your messages and the agents' replies, session titles, branches and folders, and the file paths and commands a session touched. Raw tool output isn't stored. The folder is readable only by you and excluded from Time Machine backups.
- Before storing text, Zentty replaces common API keys and tokens with `‹redacted›`: `sk-` keys, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe and npm tokens, Google API keys, AWS access key IDs, JWTs, PEM private keys and `Authorization: Bearer` values. It matches by pattern, so anything without a known shape is stored as written. That includes passwords, AWS secret keys and credentials inside connection strings. Exclude folders that hold secrets.
- When an agent deletes one of its transcripts, the session leaves the index too. Claude Code deletes conversations after 30 days unless `cleanupPeriodDays` says otherwise. If it keeps them for less than a year, the Sources list offers **Keep 1 Year**, which sets `cleanupPeriodDays` to 365 in Claude Code's `settings.json` after saving a `settings.json.zentty-backup-…` copy next to it. Zentty changes that file only when you click the button, and doesn't offer it when your organization manages the setting.
- Turning a source off removes that agent's sessions from the index. **Remove from Agent History** keeps a single session out, even after a rebuild. Settings shows how many you've removed and can restore them all.
- Turning Agent History off stops indexing and keeps the index on disk. **Delete Index and Turn Off** removes the whole `AgentHistory` folder: the index, the removed-sessions list, usage data and the on/off state. Your agents' own transcripts aren't touched. Zentty won't delete the index while another running copy of Zentty is using it.

## Bookmarks

Bookmarks store each pane's working directory as a full path. They work on both Macs when your user name and project folders match. Paths under your home folder in custom open-with apps and browsers are stored as `~/…`, so those don't depend on the user name.

If both Macs edit bookmarks at the same moment, Syncthing keeps one version and saves the other as a conflict file next to it.

## Terminal appearance

Font, colors, padding and terminal keybindings come from your Ghostty config, if you have one:

- `~/.config/ghostty/config` or `~/.config/ghostty/config.ghostty`
- `~/Library/Application Support/com.mitchellh.ghostty/config` (and `config.ghostty`)
- themes in `~/.config/ghostty/themes/`

Sync `~/.config/ghostty/` as well for identical terminals. Ghostty.app reads the same files.

The theme and background opacity you pick in Zentty's settings are always recorded in `config.toml` as well. A Mac without a Ghostty config uses those.

## Program status

Programs can set their pane's sidebar status by printing the OSC 9;4 progress sequence; see [Program Status](program-status.md). It's on by default. To turn it off:

```toml
[panes]
program_status = false
```

## Custom notification sounds

macOS only plays notification sounds from `~/Library/Sounds`. When you pick a custom sound, Zentty installs it there and keeps a copy in `~/.config/zentty/sounds/`. A Mac that receives the setting through sync installs the sound from that copy the first time it needs it.

## Replying from notifications

When an agent finishes a turn, its macOS notification has a **Reply** field. What you type is sent to the agent's prompt as one message with a single Return. The pane doesn't have to be in front. Line breaks in a reply become spaces, so a reply can't be submitted line by line.

A reply is only typed if the pane still exists, the agent is still running in it, and it is still idle after the turn the notification was raised for. If the agent has started another turn, has exited back to the shell, or the pane is gone, nothing is typed and Zentty opens the pane instead. The same happens when you reply to an older notification after turning the setting off.

Notifications for agents that need input (approvals, questions, choices, sign-in) keep **Jump to Pane** only, since the agent expects keystrokes in its own interface there.

Turn it off in Settings → Notifications, or in `config.toml`:

```toml
[notifications]
inline_reply = false
```

`GhosttyKit` is required for normal Zentty app builds. XCTest can still use mock adapters, but app builds and manual acceptance require a local `FrameworksLocal/GhosttyKit.xcframework`.

- the Zig version from `scripts/ghosttykit.lock` available locally
- `gettext` available on `PATH`
- Metal toolchain installed with Xcode

## Canonical Bootstrap Command

Run this from the repo root:

```bash

```

Expected artifact:

```text
FrameworksLocal/GhosttyKit.xcframework
```

The script also stages Ghostty resources under `~/Library/Caches/zentty/ghostty-src/zig-out/share/ghostty`.

## First Verification Checkpoint

After the framework build succeeds, confirm the app builds:

```bash
xcodebuild -project Zentty.xcodeproj -scheme Zentty -destination 'platform=macOS' build
```

`scripts/build_ghosttykit.sh` writes `FrameworksLocal/GhosttyKit.xcframework/.ghosttykit-inputs`, a fingerprint of `scripts/ghosttykit.lock` plus any `scripts/patches/ghostty-*.patch` (computed by `scripts/ghosttykit-inputs`). - `warning: GhosttyKit.xcframework has no build stamp`: the framework predates the stamp and can't be checked. Rebuild it when convenient.

If the locked Zig version is missing (currently `0.16.0`):

You do not need to relink a versioned Homebrew formula; `scripts/build_ghosttykit.sh` resolves the locked version directly.

## Updating Patched GhosttyKit

Zentty currently builds GhosttyKit from Peter's fork at `dedene/ghostty`, branch `zentty/smooth-scroll`. The lock file records both the patched revision and the official Ghostty base revision.

To update to a newer upstream Ghostty:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:dedene/ghostty.git /tmp/ghostty-zentty-update
cd /tmp/ghostty-zentty-update
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty.git
git fetch upstream
git checkout -B zentty/smooth-scroll <new-upstream-commit>
git cherry-pick <smooth-scroll-commit-range>
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Demit-macos-app=false -Dxcframework-target=universal
git push --force-with-lease origin zentty/smooth-scroll
```

Then update `scripts/ghosttykit.lock`:

- `revision` is the new `zentty/smooth-scroll` commit.
- `upstream_revision` is the official Ghostty commit used as the base.
- `repo` stays `https://github.com/dedene/ghostty.git`.

Smooth-scroll guard rows are captured as `RenderState` overscan rows (upstream #14400), so render row `y` is viewport row `y - viewportStart()`. The fork maps cursor, preedit and hyperlink coordinates accordingly; link underlines used to need a separate build-time patch for this. To run the fork's smooth-scroll regressions, including the link mapping:

```bash
zig build test -Dtest-filter='smooth scroll' -Demit-macos-app=false
```

To reproduce visually, run `scripts/repro-hyperlink-underline` inside Zentty. It prints ordinary URLs and OSC 8 links into scrollback. Scroll by a fraction of a text row, then hold Cmd while hovering each link. The underline must follow the link's text row; repeat with smooth scrolling disabled for comparison.

The downstream audit range should stay small:

```bash
git log --oneline <upstream_revision>..zentty/smooth-scroll
```

It should contain only Zentty's smooth-scroll patch stack, the embedder-vsync patch, and any direct conflict-resolution commits.

The embedder-vsync patch (`feat(zentty): let the embedder drive vsync instead of CVDisplayLink`) adds the `vsync_request_cb` runtime callback and `ghostty_surface_vsync_tick`. On macOS 14+ Zentty sets the callback and drives each surface from an `NSView.displayLink` (`LibghosttyVsyncDriver`), so libghostty never creates a CVDisplayLink. CoreVideo stops running CVDisplayLinks from its display-reconfiguration callback on the main thread, and that stop can hang forever (issue #131, ghostty-org/ghostty#14150). Keep this patch when rebasing until upstream stops using CVDisplayLink.

# Program Status

Any program can set its pane's status in the sidebar by printing one escape sequence. There's no CLI to call, no hook to install and no manifest to write. Because the sequence is plain terminal output, it works the same from a remote program over ssh.

Zentty reads the OSC 9;4 progress sequence that many tools already print:

```
ESC ] 9 ; 4 ; <state> [ ; <percent> ] BEL
```

`ST` (`ESC \`) works in place of `BEL`.

| State | Meaning | Sidebar |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | Remove | Status cleared |
| `1` | Progress, with an optional percentage (0–100) | Running, with a progress ring when a percentage is given |
| `2` | Error | Error |
| `3` | Working, no percentage | Running |
| `4` | Paused | Paused, needs attention |

## Examples

Print these from inside a running program or script. At an interactive prompt the command ends right away, and the returning prompt clears a running or paused status before you see it (an error stays).

```sh
printf '\033]9;4;3\007'      # working
printf '\033]9;4;1;42\007'   # working, 42%
printf '\033]9;4;2\007'      # error
printf '\033]9;4;4\007'      # paused, needs attention
printf '\033]9;4;0\007'      # clear
```

To try one by hand, keep the command alive for a moment:

```sh
printf '\033]9;4;1;42\007'; sleep 10
```

Wrap a command so its pane shows it running, and shows an error if it fails. This works in bash and zsh:

```sh
with_status() {
  printf '\033]9;4;3\007'
  "$@"
  rc=$?
  if [ "$rc" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf '\033]9;4;0\007'
  else
    printf '\033]9;4;2\007'
  fi
  return "$rc"
}

with_status make test
```

Report a percentage from a loop (bash and zsh):

```sh
total=${#files[@]}
i=0
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  printf '\033]9;4;1;%d\007' $(( i * 100 / total ))
  process "$f"
  i=$(( i + 1 ))
done
printf '\033]9;4;0\007'
```

## How it shows up

- **Running** shows the working indicator on the pane's sidebar row. A percentage below 100 adds a progress ring; hover it for the exact value.
- **Paused** marks the pane as needing attention.
- **Error** marks the pane with an error.

Program status is for panes that don't run an agent. When an agent reports its own status, through hooks or the [Agent Status Protocol](agent-status-protocol.md), the agent's status wins and the sequence is ignored.

## When it clears

- The program prints state `0`.
- The program prints a new state, which replaces the current one.
- The shell prompt comes back. Running and paused clear. An error stays so you can see what failed, and clears once you run the next command.
- You press Return in the pane. Paused and error clear; running stays, because programs read input while they run.
- You press Ctrl+C in the pane.
- A running status gets no new sequence for 5 minutes, unless the shell reports that the command is still running locally. This keeps a program that died without the prompt coming back (for example, over ssh, or in a shell without shell integration) from leaving a spinner behind. A remote job that wants to keep its status should repeat the sequence more often than that; printing an updated percentage counts.

Clearing on prompt return needs Zentty's shell integration in that shell. Without it, state `0` and the timeout still apply.

## Attention

When a pane turns to error or paused, Zentty adds an entry to the notification inbox. If you aren't looking at that pane, it also posts a system notification, using your notification sound settings.

## Turning it off

Set `program_status = false` under `[panes]` in `~/.config/zentty/config.toml`:

```toml
[panes]
program_status = false
```

Turning it off also clears any program status that's showing.

# Algorithm & Architecture

How FuzzyMatch turns a query and candidate into a ranked score.

## Overview

FuzzyMatch supports two matching algorithms — **Edit Distance** (default) and **Smith-Waterman** — both sharing the same prefilter pipeline and zero-allocation architecture. The algorithm is selected via ``MatchConfig/algorithm``.

### Edit Distance Pipeline

```
Candidate → Length Filter → Bitmask Filter → Trigram Filter → Edit Distance
                                                                    ↓
                                                            Position Finding
                                                                    ↓
                                              Bonus Calculation (boundaries, consecutive, gaps)
                                                                    ↓
                                                         Subsequence Fallback
                                                                    ↓
                                                          Acronym Matching
                                                                    ↓
                                                              Final Score
```

If edit distance matching fails (too many edits), a subsequence matching fallback handles abbreviation-style queries like "gubi" → "getUserById". Acronym matching then checks if the query matches word-initial characters (e.g., "bms" → "Bristol-Myers Squibb").

### Smith-Waterman Pipeline

```
Candidate → Bitmask Filter (tolerance 0) → Lowercase + Bonus Precomputation
                                                         ↓
                                              Smith-Waterman DP (single pass)
                                                         ↓
                                                  Acronym Fallback
                                                         ↓
                                              Normalize to 0.0–1.0
```

Smith-Waterman uses a single DP pass where each matched character earns points with bonuses for word boundaries, camelCase, and consecutive runs, minus affine gap penalties. Multi-word queries are split into atoms scored independently with AND semantics.

## Damerau-Levenshtein Edit Distance

The core algorithm measures the minimum number of single-character edits to transform one string into another:

| Operation | Example | Cost |
|-----------|---------|------|
| Insertion | "cat" → "cart" | 1 |
| Deletion | "cart" → "cat" | 1 |
| Substitution | "cat" → "bat" | 1 |
| Transposition | "teh" → "the" | 1 |

Standard Levenshtein treats transpositions as two operations. Damerau-Levenshtein recognizes that swapping adjacent characters is a common typo and counts it as one edit — studies show ~80% of human spelling errors are single-character edits.

The implementation uses a rolling-array dynamic programming approach with three rows (current, previous, and two-back for transpositions), reducing space from O(nm) to O(m).

### Prefix and Substring Matching

FuzzyMatch supports two edit distance modes:

- **Prefix**: Matches the query against the beginning of the candidate. Trailing candidate characters are ignored.
- **Substring**: Matches the query anywhere within the candidate by resetting the DP row at each position.

The scorer tries prefix first, falls back to substring if the prefix score is weak (below 0.7).

## Three-Stage Prefiltering

Computing edit distance is O(nm), so FuzzyMatch uses fast prefilters to reject most candidates cheaply.

### Stage 1: Length Bounds — O(1)

If the candidate is shorter than `queryLength - effectiveMaxEditDistance`, it would require more deletions than allowed. The `effectiveMaxEditDistance` is tightened for short queries (e.g., a 4-char query with `maxEditDistance=2` gets an effective value of 1). No upper bound is enforced to support subsequence matching of short queries against long candidates.

### Stage 2: Character Bitmask — O(1)

A 64-bit bitmask tracks character presence (a-z, 0-9, underscore, plus 2-byte UTF-8 characters hashed into the upper bits). The number of distinct missing character types must be within an adaptive tolerance:

```
missingChars = queryMask & ~candidateMask
bitmaskTolerance = queryLength <= 3 ? 0 : effectiveMaxEditDistance
pass = (popcount(missingChars) <= bitmaskTolerance)
```

For queries of 4+ characters, this allows substitution typos (where a character in the query is replaced by a different character in the candidate) while still quickly rejecting candidates that are too different. For example, "hein" can match "heia" (one missing character type, within `bitmaskTolerance` of 1) but a query with three missing character types would be rejected.

For very short queries (≤3 characters), the tolerance is 0 (strict): with only 1-3 distinct character types, allowing even one missing type lets nearly everything through, defeating the purpose of the prefilter. This means substitution typos (e.g., "UES" for "USD") are not detected for short queries, but transposition typos (e.g., "UDS" for "USD") still work because they involve the same character set.

### Stage 3: Trigram Similarity — O(n)

Trigrams are consecutive 3-character sequences. The candidate must share at least `queryTrigramCount - 3 * effectiveMaxEditDistance` trigrams with the query. Each edit can destroy up to 3 trigrams (a transposition at position i affects trigrams at i-2..i, i-1..i+1, and i..i+2), hence the factor of 3. This filter is only applied for queries of 4+ characters whose trigram count exceeds the tolerance threshold. Space-containing trigrams are excluded at computation time, so multi-word queries still pass through the filter.

## Scoring Model

### Base Score

Edit distance is converted to a 0.0–1.0 score:

```
baseScore = max(0, 1.0 - editDistance / queryLength)
```

### Match Type Weighting

An asymptotic formula boosts prefix matches while ensuring perfect matches always score 1.0 and imperfect matches always stay below 1.0:

```
weightedScore = max(0, 1.0 - (1.0 - baseScore) / weight)
```

### Scoring Bonuses

Position-based bonuses improve ranking quality:

- **Word boundary bonus** — Rewards matches at camelCase transitions, underscores, and digit boundaries. Query "gubi" matching "getUserById" at positions g, U, B, I gets 4 × 0.1 = 0.4 bonus.
- **Consecutive bonus** — Rewards sequential character matches. "get" matching positions 0, 1, 2 gets 2 × 0.05 = 0.1 bonus.
- **Gap penalty** — Penalizes scattered matches. The default affine model charges more to *start* a gap than to continue one, encouraging either tight matches or accepting larger structural gaps.
- **First match position bonus** — Rewards matches starting early in the candidate, decaying linearly from full value at position 0 to zero at `firstMatchBonusRange`.
- **Contiguous substring recovery** — For short queries (2–4 chars), when the greedy position finder returns scattered positions but an exact contiguous match exists, a full scan replaces the positions with the actual contiguous occurrence, preferring whole-word-bounded positions. This ensures short keyword queries like "SRI" find the actual word "SRI" at position 16 in "iShares MSCI EM SRI" rather than scattering across "i**s**ha**r**es msc**i**".
- **Whole-word substring recovery** — When a substring match is an exact, complete word (bounded by word boundaries or string edges on both sides), a portion of the length penalty is recovered using `min(lengthPenalty × 0.8, 0.15)`. This mirrors the exact prefix recovery and ensures that, for example, "SRI" as a standalone word in a long candidate beats "SERVICENOW" (shorter but mid-word match).

All bonuses are computed using a DP-optimal alignment that considers word boundaries, consecutive runs, and gaps simultaneously to find the best possible positioning.

## Subsequence Matching Fallback

When edit distance exceeds the threshold, FuzzyMatch tries subsequence matching: finding all query characters in order within the candidate, preferring word boundary positions. This handles abbreviation patterns like "gubi" → "**g**et**U**ser**B**y**I**d".

The subsequence score is based on the gap ratio between matched positions, with the same bonuses applied on top.

## Acronym Matching

When both edit distance and subsequence matching fail to produce strong results, FuzzyMatch tries acronym matching as a final pass. This handles abbreviation-style queries where users type the first letter of each word in a multi-word name (e.g., "bms" → "Bristol-Myers Squibb").

The acronym pass:
1. Checks the candidate has at least 3 words (via `popcount(boundaryMask)` — O(1) early exit)
2. Extracts the first character of each word using the precomputed boundary mask
3. Verifies the query is a subsequence of the initials
4. Scores by coverage: `score = (0.55 + 0.4 × coverage) × acronymWeight`

Where `coverage = queryLength / initialCount`. Full coverage (all initials matched) scores 0.95; partial coverage scales down proportionally. This pass runs only for queries of 2–8 characters.

## Smith-Waterman Local Alignment

The Smith-Waterman mode uses a bonus-driven approach inspired by nucleo and fzf: instead of measuring how many edits are needed, it finds the optimal local alignment of query characters within the candidate and scores it based on match quality.

### Integer DP

The inner loop uses Int32 arithmetic exclusively, avoiding floating-point in the hot path. Three parallel rows track:

- **Match row** — Score if the current candidate position is matched consecutively
- **Gap row** — Score if there's a gap before the current candidate position
- **Bonus row** — Carried consecutive bonus from the start of the current match run

Diagonal values are carried as scalar variables during the inner loop, so no row-swap logic is needed.

### Scoring Model

Each matched character earns ``SmithWatermanConfig/scoreMatch`` points (default: 16). Bonuses are added based on position context:

| Bonus | Default | Trigger |
|-------|---------|---------|
| Whitespace boundary | 10 | After space/tab, or position 0 |
| Delimiter boundary | 9 | After `/`, `:`, `;`, `\|` |
| General boundary | 8 | After non-alphanumeric characters |
| camelCase transition | 5 | Lowercase → uppercase or non-digit → digit |
| Consecutive | 4 | Adjacent matched characters |
| First char multiplier | 2× | Applied to the first matched character's bonus |

Gaps incur affine penalties: ``SmithWatermanConfig/penaltyGapStart`` (default: 3) to open, ``SmithWatermanConfig/penaltyGapExtend`` (default: 1) per additional character.

### Consecutive Bonus Propagation

When characters match consecutively at a word boundary, the boundary bonus is carried forward through the entire consecutive run (nucleo-style). This makes boundary-aligned runs significantly more valuable than scattered boundary matches.

### Multi-Word Atom Splitting

When ``SmithWatermanConfig/splitSpaces`` is `true` (default), queries containing spaces are split into independent atoms. Each atom is scored separately against the candidate with AND semantics — all atoms must match for a result. This handles queries like "johnson johnson" or "ishares treasury" naturally.

### Normalization

The raw integer score is normalized to 0.0–1.0 by dividing by a theoretical maximum (the score a perfect query-length match would achieve with full boundary bonuses and consecutive runs). This ensures scores are comparable across different query lengths.

### Acronym Fallback

For single-word queries of 2–8 characters, Smith-Waterman mode includes an acronym fallback that competes with the DP score. If the acronym score is higher, it wins. This ensures abbreviation queries like "bms" → "Bristol-Myers Squibb" work in both modes.

## Choosing a Matching Mode

| Factor | Edit Distance | Smith-Waterman |
|--------|--------------|----------------|
| Typo tolerance | Excellent (Damerau-Levenshtein) | Limited (no edit distance) |
| Multi-word queries | Basic (single alignment) | Excellent (atom splitting) |
| Throughput | Good (~26M/sec) | Higher (~44M/sec) |
| Match types | exact, prefix, substring, acronym | alignment, acronym |
| Scoring model | Penalty-driven (distance → score) | Bonus-driven (alignment → score) |
| Best for | Autocomplete, typo-tolerant search | Code/file search, high throughput |

## Complexity

| Operation | Time | Space |
|-----------|------|-------|
| Query preparation | O(q) | O(q) |
| Length + bitmask filter | O(1) | O(1) |
| Trigram filter | O(c) | O(1) |
| Edit distance | O(q × c) | O(q) |
| ED bonus calculation | O(q × c) | O(q × c) |
| Smith-Waterman DP | O(q × c) | O(q) |
| Acronym matching | O(c) | O(1) |

Where q = query length, c = candidate length. In practice, prefilters reject most candidates in O(1), so the amortized cost per candidate is very low.

# Quality & Performance

How FuzzyMatch compares to established fuzzy matchers and what to expect from its performance.

## Overview

FuzzyMatch has been compared against established fuzzy matching implementations — [fzf](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) (Go), [nucleo](https://github.com/helix-editor/nucleo) (Rust), [RapidFuzz](https://github.com/rapidfuzz/rapidfuzz-cpp) (C++), and [Ifrit](https://github.com/ukushu/Ifrit) (Swift) — on a corpus of 272K financial instruments across 197 test queries. The quality comparison below uses the default edit distance mode. See [COMPARISON.md](https://github.com/ordo-one/FuzzyMatch/blob/main/COMPARISON.md) for full results including Smith-Waterman mode.

## Quality Comparison

| Metric | FuzzyMatch | nucleo | fzf |
|--------|-----------|--------|-----|
| Queries returning results | **197/197** | 190/197 | 186/197 |
| Top-1 agreement with fzf | **129/197** | 87/197 | — |

FuzzyMatch achieves the highest hit rate among precision-focused matchers and the highest pairwise agreement with fzf (65%), the de facto standard for fuzzy search.

### Typo Handling

FuzzyMatch's Damerau-Levenshtein foundation handles transposition typos that other matchers miss entirely:

| Query (typo) | FuzzyMatch | nucleo | fzf |
|--------------|-----------|--------|-----|
| "Voeing" (B→V adjacent) | Found | Not found | Not found |
| "Gokdman Sachs" (l→k adjacent) | Found | Not found | Not found |
| "Govenrment" | Found | Found | Found |
| "isahres" | Found | Found | Found |

### Abbreviation Handling

FuzzyMatch's acronym matching pass finds the correct company for 7/12 abbreviation queries, outperforming all other matchers:

| Query | FuzzyMatch | nucleo | fzf |
|-------|-----------|--------|-----|
| "bms" → Bristol-Myers Squibb | **Found** | Not found | Not found |
| "tfs" → Thermo Fisher Scientific | **Found** | **Found** | **Found** |
| "gmc" → General Motors Company | **Found** | Not found | Not found |
| "csc" → Columbia Sportswear Co | **Found** | Not found | Not found |

### Overall Assessment

| | Hit Rate | Typo Handling | Short Queries | Abbreviations | Precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FuzzyMatch** | 197/197 | Best | Good | Good (7/12) | High |
| **fzf** | 186/197 | None | Good | Poor (2/12) | High |
| **nucleo** | 190/197 | Decent | Poor | Poor (2/12) | Medium |

### Smith-Waterman Mode

In Smith-Waterman mode, FuzzyMatch trades typo tolerance for higher throughput and nucleo-compatible rankings:

| Metric | FuzzyMatch (ED) | FuzzyMatch (SW) | nucleo |
|--------|---------|---------|--------|
| Hit rate | **197/197** | 187/197 | 190/197 |
| Top-1 agreement with nucleo | 77/197 | **182/197** | — |
| Throughput | 32M/sec | 66M/sec | 97M/sec |

FuzzyMatch (SW) agrees with nucleo on 92% of top-1 rankings (182/197). It excels at multi-word queries and long descriptive searches, but loses 10 queries that require edit distance typo tolerance. Use Smith-Waterman mode when you need maximum throughput or nucleo-compatible behavior; use the default edit distance mode when typo tolerance matters.

## Performance

FuzzyMatch processes ~32 million candidates per second in edit distance mode and ~66 million in Smith-Waterman mode on Apple Silicon (M4 Max). While nucleo (Rust, Smith-Waterman variant) is 1.2–4.5x faster in raw throughput, both FuzzyMatch modes comfortably handle interactive-speed search:

| | Throughput |
|---|---|
| nucleo (Rust) | ~97M candidates/sec |
| FuzzyMatch — SW (Swift) | ~66M candidates/sec |

## Unicode Support

FuzzyMatch supports case-insensitive matching for ASCII, Latin-1 Supplement (Ä→ä, Ö→ö, Å→å), Greek (Α→α, Σ→σ, Ω→ω), and basic Cyrillic (А→а, Я→я, Ё→ё). Greek and Cyrillic support is provided as a courtesy for users who need these scripts, but they are not a primary target for the package. All string processing operates on raw UTF-8 bytes — custom byte-level case folding is used instead of Swift's `String.lowercased()` to avoid per-call allocations in the hot scoring path. An ASCII fast path skips multi-byte dispatch for the vast majority of candidates, maintaining full throughput on ASCII-dominant corpora.

Two kinds of normalization are applied during matching:
- **Diacritic normalization** — Latin-1 diacritics fold to ASCII base letters (`café` → `cafe`); combining marks (U+0300–U+036F) are stripped
- **Confusable-character normalization** — visually similar punctuation and whitespace collapse to canonical ASCII forms (curly quotes → `'`, en-dash → `-`, NBSP → space, ʻokina → `'`)

Both matching modes share the same UTF-8 processing, case folding, and normalization. See [DAMERAU_LEVENSHTEIN.md](https://github.com/ordo-one/FuzzyMatch/blob/main/Documentation/DAMERAU_LEVENSHTEIN.md#unicode-support) for the full list of supported scripts and byte-level semantics.

## Zero-Allocation Design

The high-performance API (``FuzzyMatcher/score(_:against:buffer:)``) performs zero heap allocations when using prepared queries and reusable buffers. This is achieved through:

- **Prepared queries** — ``FuzzyQuery`` precomputes lowercased bytes, bitmask, and trigrams once
- **Reusable buffers** — ``ScoringBuffer`` holds pre-allocated arrays for DP rows, candidate bytes, and match positions
- **Automatic memory management** — Buffers grow when needed and periodically shrink when recent usage is much smaller than allocated capacity

This design is critical for responsive UI and high-throughput batch processing scenarios.

### Choosing the Right API

FuzzyMatch provides three API tiers that produce identical results:

| API | When to use | Allocations | Throughput |
|-----|-------------|-------------|------------|
| ``FuzzyMatcher/score(utf8:against:buffer:)`` | Maximum throughput hot paths | Zero (after buffer warmup) | Highest (~60% faster on Swift 6.0) |
| ``FuzzyMatcher/score(_:against:buffer:)`` | Production hot paths with String inputs | Zero (after buffer warmup) | High |
| ``FuzzyMatcher/score(_:against:)`` | One-off checks, prototyping | Per-call (buffer + query) | — |
| ``FuzzyMatcher/topMatches(_:against:limit:)-(_,FuzzyQuery,_)`` | Quick top-N results | Per-call (buffer) | — |
| ``FuzzyMatcher/matches(_:against:)-(_,FuzzyQuery)`` | Quick sorted results | Per-call (buffer) | — |

The ``FuzzyMatcher/score(utf8:against:buffer:)`` method is `@inlinable` and accepts `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>` directly, enabling cross-module inlining. On Swift 6.0, `String.withUTF8` is non-inlinable, which prevents the optimizer from inlining through the String overload. This gap will be resolved when the library adopts Swift 6.2+ Span.

The convenience methods (``FuzzyMatcher/score(_:against:)``, ``FuzzyMatcher/topMatches(_:against:limit:)-(_,String,_)``, ``FuzzyMatcher/matches(_:against:)-(_,String)``) allocate a buffer internally on each call. For scoring loops over many candidates, the high-performance API with an explicit buffer avoids this overhead entirely.
